stories.headline: Self-listing of bourses feasible, says NSE chief
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Self-listing by stock exchanges is feasible, but the decision remains under the purview of market regulator Sebi, NSE chairperson Srinivas Injeti said Friday. A day after the country's largest bourse got listed on rival exchange 
BSE
, Injeti pitched for self-listing, saying that things which are not permitted today may be allowed tomorrow amid evolving regulations.
Current regulations do not allow self-listing or trading of the shares of an exchange on its own platform. In compliance with present norms, NSE shares are listed on BSE and vice versa.
"Self-listing may not be permitted today, but may be permitted tomorrow. It is (allowing to do so) something which is the regulator's prerogative," Injeti said at a media briefing here. "There is no problem. But, this (self-listing) is something which is in the realm of feasibility... it is feasible," he said. Injeti also mentioned that allowing or not allowing self-listing depends on the comfort and concerns of Sebi.
Once such a move is permitted, and NSE is able to meet requirements adequately to satisfaction of the regulator, then self-listing may become reality. According to him, things which were not permitted in the past are now allowed, and things that are not approved today may be permissible tomorrow, as he cited the example of listing of Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs). 
Listing of MIIs was not allowed prior to 2012 but was approved and sort of operationalised in 2015, he added.
"The difference is that if you have self-listing, you will also be regulating yourself in terms of LODR compliance and even the surveillance part. And, if it is a permission to trade, then that exchange, in this case (our own platform), will not have the regulatory obligation of monitoring the companies. The regulated exchange will be doing that," Injeti said. agencies

stories.headline: Indian economy doing well amid global headwinds, says RBI
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: RBI on Friday said the Indian economy has performed well despite global headwinds and noted that escalation of West Asia conflict this month has resulted in a sharp increase in oil prices, reigniting fears over a build-up of inflationary pressure and further disruption in supply chains.
The central bank's latest RBI Bulletin also said strong FCNR(B) deposits led to brief recoveries in the rupee in early Sept, but the gains reversed in later part of the month on account of higher crude prices. It stated that high level of surplus liquidity in the system following $133 billion FCNR(B) flows can support the ongoing credit growth, driven by acceleration in credit flow to industry. It also said that in Aug, bank deposits grew at their fastest pace in 15 years, resulting in a moderation in incremental credit deposit ratio.
"Despite such a challenging global environment, the Indian economy recorded a strong GDP growth in Q1 of 2026-27. High-frequency indicators through Aug reflected sustained demand, with segments of industry and services sectors displaying resilience... India's financial and external sectors are drawing strength from the real economy, although geopolitical tensions and weather-related uncertainties are acting as key downside risks," RBI said in its 'State of the Economy" report.
 It said that most high frequency indicators remained healthy in Aug.
It, however, cautioned that rise in sovereign yields in some of the major advanced economies has put pressure on govt finances.
Gross, net FDI rise
Latest data released by RBI estimated that net FDI jumped 64% to $7.3 billion in July, on the back of robust gross inflows of $14.6 billion, which was an increase of over 31% over a year ago. Communication, financial and computer services were the major sectors, receiving more than four-fifths of the equity inflows (see graphic). Mauritius, the UAE, and the US were the major source countries, accounting for about 70% of equity inflows, RBI said. During April-July, net inflows were 38% higher at $13.4 billion, while gross FDI rose 12.6% to $43.9 billion.
On the other hand, after declining for two months, overseas investments also rose 26% in July to $3.4 billion. RBI said over two-thirds of outward FDI flows went to Singapore, the UK, and the UAE, with financial, insurance and business services, and manufacturing accounting for about two-thirds of the outward flows.

briefs.headline: India should allow exchanges to list on own platform, NSE chairman says
briefs.deck: NSE accounts for about 93% of India’s cash-market ⁠trading and nearly 75% of options
briefs.bodyText:
India’s markets regulator should reconsider allowing exchanges to list on their own platforms, NSE Chairman Srinivas Injeti said on Friday (September 25, 2026), a day after the bourse operator debutedon rival BSE at a valuation of about $47 billion.
India’s markets regulator debated allowing self-listing in 2015 but rejected the idea over potential conflicts of interest, requiring their shares to trade on rival bourses.
However, self-listing is permitted in several major global markets. In the United States for example, the New York Stock Exchange’s parent Intercontinental Exchange is listed and traded on the NYSE, which it operates.
NSE accounts for about 93% of India’s cash-market trading and nearly 75% of options.
Impact on options volume is largely over
The world’s busiest derivatives exchange listed as investors grow wary of slowing volumes and its reliance on options for growth.
Options trading has declined after tighter regulation and rule changes aimed at aligning Indian markets with global standards.
“Whatever volumes had to go down due to regulatory changes to cool down derivatives trading and due to teething issues due to closing auction session have already gone down,” Ashish Chauhan, chief executive, NSE said in an interview with Reuters on Friday (September 25, 2026).
“Volumes are still high and spread across many instruments including monthly options which are pretty large,” mR. Chauhan said.
New growth avenues
The Securities and Exchange Board of India has sought to curb speculative options trading by raising costs while encouraging growth in the cash market.
Chauhan said NSE would help develop the cash market if the government set out that objective through regulation.
Allowing foreign portfolio investors to trade bullion contracts would also help NSE grow its commodities business, Chief Business Officer Sriram Krishnan said.
India on Thursday permitted FPIs to participate in physically settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives, a move expected to boost trading volumes in bullion contracts by broadening the investor base and bringing the market more in line with global peers.
FPIs will be able to use capital already allocated for equity investments to trade in commodity derivatives, Krishnan said.
He added that slowly both commodities and data monetisation will evolve from peripheral activities into standalone revenue generators.

briefs.headline: Govt evaluating financial bids for IDBI Bank strategic sale: Sources
briefs.bodyText:
The government is evaluating the financial bids for strategic stake sale in IDBI Bank and the process is moving at a steady pace, government sources said on Friday (September 25, 2026).
In July, billionaire investor Prem Watsa-backed Fairfax Financial Holdings and Dubai-based Emirates NBD had put in their revised bids to buy 60.72% in IDBI Bank, sources had earlier said.
The strategic disinvestment of IDBI Bank is moving at a steady pace. The government is evaluating the financial bids submitted by the interested investors, the sources said, without disclosing any further details.
Both the bidders have experience in the Indian banking sector, with Dubai-based Emirates NDB acquiring majority stake in RBL Bank earlier this year and Fairfax Financial holding a 40% stake in the private-sector CSB Bank.
The bidders already have security clearance from Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and 'Fit and Proper' assessment from the Reserve Bank of India.
This is the second time that the interested bidders have put in financial bids for buying stake in IDBI Bank, in which the government and Life Insurance Corporation (LIC) are together looking to sell 60.72%.
An Expression of Interest (EoI) for the strategic sale was floated in October 2022, and after regulatory clearances and due diligence, financial bids came in on February 6, 2026. However, the bids by Fairfax Financial Holdings and Emirates NBD came in below the reserve price decided by the Inter-ministerial group on disinvestment headed by secretaries in the finance ministry. The government then put the strategic sale process on hold.
The strategic sale process restarted this financial year and the government invited revised financial bids from the two suitors early in July. The revised financial bids came in on July 13, 2026.
Currently, the government and state-owned LIC together hold 94.71% stake in IDBI Bank. The government owns 45.48%, while LIC holds 49.24% in the lender.
Of this, the government and LIC are looking to sell 60.72% — the Centre's 30.48 and LIC's 30.24% stake, respectively.

briefs.headline: Ties with US in 'uneasy equilibrium': CEA
briefs.bodyText:
India's relationship with the US is in an "uneasy equilibrium" as trade disputes between the partners persist, a senior govt official said. "There is this issue of unsettled relationship with the US, starting from the tariff-related issues last year, which are still continuing," chief economic adviser V Anantha Nageswaran said in a speech at SBI's banking and economics conclave in Mumbai on Thursday.
New Delhi faces a fresh tariff threat even after reaching an interim trade deal with Washington earlier this year. A new US law gives President Donald Trump the power to impose levies of as much as 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas, adding uncertainty as India and the US negotiate a final tariff rate. Nageswaran said the trade and energy pressures facing India may also reflect a broader push to choose between rival global blocs. "India, given its geography and its size, cannot obviously belong to any bloc," Nageswaran said, adding that maintaining its independence could come at cost of higher energy prices and periodic supply disruptions. bloomberg

briefs.headline: No extra time for realising export proceeds
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: With the rupee under pressure, the RBI has rolled back an earlier move to give exporters more time to bring in export proceeds from Oct 2026. In Jan, the RBI had allowed exporters 15 months from the date of shipment or invoice to realise and repatriate the proceeds from Oct. The Sept amendment retains the existing nine month limit for future.
The RBI has made a similar change for goods exported to overseas warehouses, cutting the period from 15 months to nine months from the date of sale. For exports invoiced or settled in Indian rupees, the timeline has been reduced to 12 months from 18 months. The Jan regulations had provided the longer 18-month window with effect from Oct.
The latest amendment does not remove the flexibility available to exporters facing delays. Authorised dealers can still extend the deadline if an exporter provides reasons for the delay and the bank is satisfied with them.

briefs.headline: India may sign new investment pact with Australia & Canada
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The new model bilateral investment treaty (BIT), which will address concerns of several countries and streamline investment negotiation procedures, while ensuring investor protection is in final stage and is likely to be approved by govt soon. The approval will pave the way for it to be rolled out along with trade agreements, with countries such as Australia and Canada, while also being used with partners such as the UK and the European Union.
One of the key elements is reduction in the period to seek international arbitration to one year from five years at present, provided domestic remedies are exhausted.
"The finance ministry has sent the draft note for approval and it will be approved soon. There are a few red lines, which are not being given up. The new BIT will continue to protect India's sovereign rights on taxation and domestic courts. No tax related provisions will be part of it as it is a Parliamentary prerogative," a senior official said. The Union cabinet is expected to approve the revised model BIT over next couple of weeks, replacing the contentious version of 2015, which was rejected by most countries.
According to Unctad database, since 2018 only six countries have agreed to BITs with India, including Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, Brazil, UAE, Uzbekistan and Israel. India has already made concessions in case of UAE and Israel, while refusing to make any exception for the UK, EU or the four-nation European Free Trade Association and others with which trade agreements have been signed.
"Under the previous framework, negotiations took place with 20-25 countries. Recent negotiations with countries such as UAE, Qatar and Oman have already diverged from that framework. India is currently negotiating BITs with four countries, including Canada and UK. And, these will be done under the new framework," the official said.
On Friday, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said full FTA with Australia, which is under negotiaton, will come with an investment pact. "Now we have decided to work towards a very balanced, fair and equitable, comprehensive economic cooperation agreement, which will also take our relationship to greater heights. We are working with Australia to have a bilateral investment treaty also." A BIT is an agreement between two countries to promote and protect investments made by their investors in each other's territory. Under investment protection treaties, investors can take a sovereign govt to arbitration.

briefs.headline: Festive sales: Cos paying retention bonus to workers
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: The festive bonus is no longer always one big cheque at the end of a busy month. For workers packing orders, staffing stores or delivering parcels, the extra money can now come through a higher rate on a busy day, an attendance reward after a week, a productivity payout or a bonus for staying through the entire sale season.
As ecommerce, retail and logistics companies ramp up for the year's biggest shopping period, competition for frontline workers is increasingly becoming a retention battle. Companies are putting greater emphasis on incentives tied to attendance, performance and completing the festive season, even as the actual boost to workers' take-home pay can depend heavily on targets and hours worked.
TeamLease Services said spending on festive incentives rose 15-20% in 2025 over 2024 and this year more of the incentive pool this year is being directed towards longer-duration retention payouts for weekly or monthly attendance and end-of-season completion bonuses. "Daily surge pay still exists, but it increasingly sits on top of milestone-based rewards," said Balasubramanian A, senior vice-president at TeamLease Services.
The shift reflects cost of workers leaving midway through peak demand. Festive attrition in high-pressure frontline roles was 35-40% last year, TeamLease said. Last season, monthly earnings across warehouse, fulfilment, picking and packing roles were 12-15% above normal months in metros and 18-22% higher in Tier-II markets, largely due to variable pay.
The premium is visible outside warehouses too. Timbuckdo, which connects college students with part-time jobs, said one retailer hiring through its platform can raise pay from around Rs 110 an hour on regular days to about Rs 150 during high-footfall sale periods, taking daily earnings in one example from roughly Rs 600 to Rs 900.
Myntra, which is creating over 26,000 seasonal jobs for its Big Fashion Festival, said its reward system continues to include daily spot awards such as electronic gift vouchers or goodies for top-performing fulfilment-centre employees.
Flipkart said its delivery workers are being offered joining and retention bonuses as well as referral incentives this festive season, alongside insurance and healthcare benefits.

briefs.headline: Centre to borrow nearly Rs 7.9 lakh cr in Oct-March
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Govt will raise nearly Rs 7.9 lakh crore from securities in the second half of this fiscal year, reducing the total borrowing for the current financial year by Rs 1,20,494 crore despite global headwinds.
The reduction in total borrowing indicates govt's commitment to fiscal prudence.
A senior finance ministry official said the reduction is mainly due to switching G-secs maturing in 2026-27 of Rs 1,14,286 crore, a conscious debt-management strategy of govt. "During 2026-27, govt is expected to have market borrowing of Rs 15,99,506 crore through dated securities, as compared to Budget Estimates of Rs 17,20,000 crore for the ongoing financial year," the finance ministry said in a statement.
"Govt, in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), has decided to borrow Rs 7,86,000 crore in the second half (H2) of FY 2026-27. This includes Sovereign Green Bonds (SGrBs) issuance of Rs 15,000 crore," it said.
During the first half ending this month, govt would mobilise Rs 8,13,506 crore from bonds, slightly lower than the target of Rs 8.2 lakh crore, to fund the revenue gap.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the Budget presented on Feb 1 had proposed to borrow Rs 17.2 lakh crore to fund its fiscal deficit projected at 4.3% of the GDP. In absolute terms, the fiscal deficit is pegged at Rs 16.9 lakh crore for 2026-27. agencies

briefs.headline: Forex reserves decline by $15bn to $766bn
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $14.9 billion to $765.9 billion in the week ended Sept 18, according to the RBI's weekly statistical data. The decline was driven mainly by a fall in foreign currency assets (FCA), the largest component of the reserves. FCA fell by $14.8 billion to $631 billion during the week.
Gold reserves rose marginally by $68 million to $111.3 billion. Special drawing rights fell by $106 million to $18.7 billion, while India's reserve position in the IMF declined by $27 million to $4.9 billion. The weekly decline comes after a period of strong accumulation in the reserves. Since the end of March 2026, the reserves are still higher by $74.8 billion.
On a year-on-year basis, the reserves are up by $63.3 billion. Bankers said the decline could be due to dollar sales by the RBI to support the rupee. Changes in the value of major currencies held in the RBI's foreign currency assets can also affect the reserves when measured in dollar terms. tnn

stories.headline: Asiad: India’s 44-year wait ends as Barwal bags marathon silver
stories.deck: Sawan Barwal won silver in the men’s marathon at the 2026 Asian Games, ending India’s 44-year wait for a medal in the event. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita. Barwal’s silver is India’s fourth Asian Games marathon medal and follows his national-record performance earlier this year. Kartik Karkera finished 17th.
stories.bodyText:
Sawan Barwal scripted history at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday, winning silver in the men’s marathon and ending India’s 44-year wait for a medal in the event. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing 48 seconds behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita, who won gold in 2:10:49. China’s Peiyou Feng took bronze with 2:12:13.
The marathon started at 4 a.m. IST with 19 runners, including Barwal and fellow Indian Kartik Karkera. Barwal quickly established himself among the leaders and was in second place at the halfway mark with a timing of 1:05:54. He continued to hold his position as the race entered its final stages, reaching the 35-kilometre mark in second.
With around seven kilometres left, Barwal was still chasing Yamashita. The Japanese runner eventually opened up a gap, but Barwal maintained his pace and stayed firmly in silver-medal position. He finished with a timing of 2:11:37, securing India’s first Asian Games marathon medal since the 1982 Delhi Games and the country’s first medal in the event on foreign soil.
Historic medal for Indian athletics
The silver adds to Barwal’s growing record. In April, he broke Shivnath Singh’s 48-year-old national marathon record at the NN Marathon Rotterdam. 
His latest performance now converts that record-setting form into a major international medal.
Barwal’s silver is India’s fourth Asian Games marathon medal. Chhota Singh won gold and Surat Singh Mathur took bronze at the inaugural 1951 Games, while Hosur Kukkappa Seetharan won another bronze in 1982.
The other Indian runner, Kartik Karkera, finished 17th among 19 competitors with a time of 2:22:41.

stories.headline: UEFA Nations League: Mbappe scores but suffers knee injury as Zidane gets debut France win
stories.deck: ‘It’s not great; unfortunately, I think he’s going to have to go home; we don’t want to take any risks’, said Zinedine Zidane
stories.bodyText:
Kylian Mbappe scored the only goal of the game before having to come off, grimacing with a knee injury as France won 1-0 in Turkey in the UEFA Nations League in new coach Zinedine Zidane's first game in charge on Friday (September 25, 2026).
The Real Madrid superstar was moved out to the left wing by his new coach after being used through the middle of the French attack under former coach Didier Deschamps at the recent World Cup, where he ended as the top scorer with 10 goals.
It was from the left that Mbappe, France's all-time top scorer, notched his 67th international goal, controlling and firing in low at the near post after being set up by Michael Olise.
He winced in pain as his teammates came across to celebrate the goal at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, just over 100 kilometres outside Istanbul.
Mbappe tried to carry on after receiving treatment, but eventually slumped to the ground and looked concerned as he prodded the outside of his left knee, before walking off to be replaced by Desire Doue.
France and Real will now nervously wait to discover the extent of the injury, with Les Bleus playing three more games over the next 10 days before the club season resumes.
Zidane confirmed that Mbappe is now likely to return to his club for treatment.
"It's not great. Unfortunately, I think he's going to have to go home. We don't want to take any risks," Zidane told broadcaster TF1. "He overextended his knee while shooting. It's not very encouraging."
The sight of his star player and skipper coming off overshadowed Zidane's first match since being appointed coach in late July on a deal to 2030.
The France legend and 1998 World Cup winner is making his return to elite coaching for the first time since his second stint in charge of Madrid ended in 2021.
"It was a really emotional night, but it was a successful debut in difficult surroundings. I think we played rather well. I saw a lot of interesting things, considering we have only had three and a half training sessions together. It's quite encouraging," he added.
France, beaten in the semi-finals at the World Cup by eventual winners Spain, are in Group A1 of this edition of the Nations League and will now go to Brussels to face Belgium on Monday. Belgium won 2-0 away to Italy on Friday.
Cherki plays
Zidane, whose last match as a player came for France against Italy in the 2006 World Cup final, will then make his home debut as coach against the Italians at the Stade de France next Friday.
His first team selection was not dramatically different to the side that regularly played at the World Cup, although Bournemouth's Adrien Truffert was in at left-back while Manchester City's Rayan Cherki came into the starting XI.
Olise, the Bayern Munich star who lit up the World Cup, was unlucky not to open the scoring late in the first half when his superb strike was tipped over by home goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir.
France goalkeeper Mike Maignan responded at the start of the second half as he tipped over an attempt by Abdulkerim Bardakci for Turkey, who finished bottom of their group at the World Cup despite a 3-2 win over co-hosts the United States.
Mbappe's goal came shortly after, and the visitors later saw Jules Kounde hit the post before Turkey were reduced to 10 men late on.

stories.headline: Saina Nehwal: “I will be happy as long as winners from non-cricket sports are also celebrated”
stories.deck: Even for the trailblazing Saina Nehwal, getting into the limelight was tough in a cricket-mad country. In a free-wheeling chat, the Olympic and World championships medallist speaks on the struggle for co-existence between sports in India, the impending change to badminton’s scoring system, P.V. Sindhu’s future and the next generation of stars.
stories.bodyText:
Saina Nehwal chuckled when asked if the 3x15 scoring system, set to come into force from January 2027, could tempt her to return to the badminton court.
In theory, Saina, at least at her peak, would have revelled in this abridged format. Her natural attacking flair, speed and ability to close out games would have made her a neat fit.
While this could make for a good debate over coffee, the reality is quite different. At 36, and having gone through the intense grind of the professional tour for nearly two decades, Saina is unable to meet the physical demands of the sport.
“I wish I could come back, but I have total cartilage damage,” she said during a virtual interaction. “My knee is in a seriously bad shape. I cannot push for more than half an hour. But yes, I really do want to play.”
Saina believes that her contemporary P.V. Sindhu will benefit from the new rules. Sindhu, 31, maybe in the final stages of her career, but has plenty of fight left. In July, the double Olympic medallist served a reminder of her class by becoming the first Indian to win the Japan Open.
Merits and demerits
“The good thing is that Sindhu has the best physiotherapist and trainer. This is really helpful. Her court movement is very good,” Saina observed.
“From next year, when the points system shifts to 3x15, matches will get shorter. You will get a lot of recovery time between fixtures. There are big breaks between Super 1000 tournaments too, which guarantees good rest periods.
“Careers will extend longer because the matches are shorter. Any player can win tournaments in that scenario,” the two-time World championships medallist added.
Saina, the first Indian woman to reach the summit in the World rankings, added a note of caution regarding training regimens.
“The new scoring system will tilt the game towards power and speed. But when you train for power and speed, chances of getting injured are higher. If Sindhu can take care to avoid injuries, she can play for a long time,” she opined.
Looking at the talent that has emerged after Saina and Sindhu, there remains a gap in quality. The likes of Unnati Hooda and Tanvi Sharma have registered some impressive wins, but are not yet world-beaters in the class of their seniors.
“In terms of attitude and skill, Tanvi and Unnati have a very bright future. They have gained experience and produced results. Devika [Sihag] and the other players need to improve a bit more.
“There are challenges – how do you make a comeback from a loss? How much do you train on a regular basis? Are you ready to push yourself and not give up? As far as I have seen, Tanvi and Unnati don’t give up. They keep fighting. They have the best coaches too. Tanvi is training under Park [Tae-sang], while Unnati is training with her father,” Saina stated.
As for the best in the world, Saina rates 2024 Paris Olympics gold medallist An Se-young as a “once in a generation” player. She had taken on the South Korean when the latter was a promising youngster, sharing the spoils with a 1-1 head-to-head record.
“An can rally very well, and the improvement now is that she dives well to pick up shots. She has also improved the speed of strokes. She is not the fastest player, but she has fast strokes and her court coverage is very smooth,” Saina said.
And then there is the 24-year-old’s intense drive – a trait Saina views as key.
“Even after having won the Olympic gold and so many titles, you can still see that hunger to win. When she lost recently, you saw her crying. A player with that sort of desire is tough to defeat.”
Against the odds
The 2012 London Olympics bronze medallist is of the opinion that with cricket taking centrestage in India, athletes in other sports must stay at an elite level to gain recognition.
“In India, the problem is that if you perform in any sport apart from cricket, you don’t get much importance unless you win tournaments. Tanvi and Unnati have won tournaments, and that’s why everyone is talking about them. You have to show results and win consistently. That is when you get popular in this country.”
Saina, who is serving on the expert panel of Sony Sports Network for its coverage of the 2026 Asian Games, is hopeful that the hype around the Indian cricket teams will not overshadow other disciplines at the multi-sport extravaganza.
“I will be happy as long as medal winners from other sports are [also] celebrated. We expect the Indian cricket team to win medals at the Asian Games and the Olympics. But this could mean that medallists from other sports might feel bad if they don’t receive the same encouragement as the cricketers.
“I have a feeling that [even] if they (non-cricket sportspersons) win a gold medal, they will get sidelined. In that scenario, I will feel bad because only cricket gets the support,” Saina explained.
The Padma Bhushan awardee reflected on the challenges she faced during her playing career, especially when it came to getting the attention of the general public.
“I had to win multiple Super Series titles in a year to be there [in the spotlight]. Just one Super Series victory was not enough. I had the motivation to win an Olympic medal, and to become the World No. 1. The victories helped me appear in newspapers, and people started to notice me.”
Guts and glory
Her groundbreaking achievements were marked by self-improvement and dedication to the sport.
“I worked on improving myself every day – listening to my coaches, thinking about how to prepare for the next tournament, staying injury-free… I had big goals for myself, which is why I was able to win at Super Series events and the World championships,” Saina stated.
“Having said that, I also feel sad that after winning 24 international titles and an Olympic medal, many people confuse me with tennis player Sania Mirza.
“I am sure that about 70 to 80% of girls in India do not know anything about the world of sports. We have to find out how we can promote sports. I am not against cricket, but other sports cann ever overtake cricket unless athletes keep winning at the highest level.”
Saina emphasised the role of a stable support system, starting with good parenting.
“To win even a couple of Super Series tournaments is very, very challenging for Indian players. If there is no financial support, we should not expect to win a single title.
“When my parents took the risk to support my badminton dreams, they did not think much about the great financial rewards I may get. They just wholeheartedly supported me, and luckily I could come back with so many good results. But how many parents can do this? It’s not that easy.”

stories.headline: India Hold Panama 1-1: Blue Tigers impress against world No.44; Brazil, Uruguay await
stories.deck: India held FIFA World Cup side Panama to a 1-1 draw in Bengaluru after Ryan Williams gave the Blue Tigers a first-half lead. Omar Valencia equalised after the break, but India created chances to win and withstood late pressure. The result offers Khalid Jamil’s side encouragement ahead of tougher friendlies against Brazil and Uruguay in October.
stories.bodyText:
India had to surrender a first-half lead, but the Blue Tigers came away from Bengaluru with plenty to take from a 1-1 draw against Panama, a side ranked 94 places above them in the FIFA rankings and featuring several players from the country’s recent World Cup campaign. Ryan Williams put India ahead shortly before half-time, only for Omar Valencia to level with a long-range strike in the second half, leaving Khalid Jamil’s side with an encouraging result against the world No. 44 team.
Williams rewards India's positive first half
Panama enjoyed more possession during the opening stages, but India stayed compact and looked increasingly dangerous when they broke forward, showing little sign of being overawed by opponents who had competed at the FIFA World Cup only a few months earlier.
India created their first clear opening in the eighth minute when Akash Mishra’s cut-back found Williams inside the penalty area, although the forward could not get his shot away. Williams went close again 10 minutes later when he dragged an effort narrowly wide, while Ashique Kuruniyan then found the side-netting as India continued to threaten.
The pressure finally produced a breakthrough in the 41st minute. Akash sent a long ball forward, Williams timed his run perfectly to get behind the Panama defence and then kept his composure to beat goalkeeper Marcos Reyes, giving India a 1-0 lead four minutes before the interval.
It was a significant moment for a team ranked 138th in the world and playing in Bengaluru for the first time since winning the SAFF Championship at the same stadium in 2023.
Panama respond, but India withstand the pressure
Panama came out with greater urgency after the restart and quickly began testing the Indian defence. Gurpreet Singh Sandhu was equal to the first major threat, producing a save to deny Giovany Herbert five minutes into the second half.
The visitors eventually found their equaliser in the 68th minute, when Valencia struck from outside the box to make it 1-1 and give Panama a platform from which to search for a winner.
India still had opportunities to reclaim the lead. Ashique sent a low cross into the box in the 79th minute, but Edmund Lalrindika was unable to make proper contact. Two minutes later, Edmund worked his way in from the right and set up Manvir Singh, who attempted to finish with a backheel rather than taking the simpler option and missed the chance.
Panama then pushed forward in search of a decisive goal, striking the woodwork and forcing Gurpreet into another important save. Carlos Harvey, one of the visitors’ World Cup players, also tested the Indian goalkeeper, but India managed to survive the late pressure.
Manvir came close again late in the match after being played in by substitute Edmund, while Abhishek Singh Tekcham fired off target following a corner as India continued to carry a threat of their own.
India now turn to Brazil and Uruguay
The 1-1 draw gives Jamil’s team an important result before a far more demanding sequence of friendlies. India will face five-time world champions Brazil in Kolkata on October 3 before meeting two-time world champions Uruguay at the same venue three days later.
For India, the significance of Friday’s result lies not simply in avoiding defeat against Panama, but in the way the Blue Tigers competed against a side ranked 44th in the world. Williams’ first-half finish gave them a lead to protect, Panama eventually found a way through, and India still created enough opportunities afterwards to believe they could have taken all three points.
The next two fixtures will provide a considerably tougher test, but the performance in Bengaluru has given Jamil’s side something substantial to carry into them.

briefs.headline: Operating in a silo or fitting into the whole – what’s in a Sprint?
briefs.deck: Introduced in 2021 as a way to jazz up the days leading up to a Formula One Grand Prix, the Sprint race has had a chequered history. Yet, for the 2027 season, the big bosses of F1 have increased its number from six to 10. What’s behind the move and how to enhance the product’s value?
briefs.bodyText:
On September 16, F1 unveiled its 2027 calendar with 24 races scheduled across five continents. Headlines from the announcement included confirmation of a return to venues like Portimao in Portugal and Istanbul in Turkey.
While the number of races has hovered around 22 to 24 in recent years, the highlight for 2027 is the increase in Sprint races from six to 10. Sprints are shortened dashes of 100 kilometres, held on Saturdays ahead of the main Grand Prix on the Sunday.
Ever since the Drive to Survive series first aired on Netflix in 2019, F1’s popularity has skyrocketed, making its races some of the best-attended sporting events in the world.
To cash in on the surge, and help race promoters get more bang for the buck, Sprints were introduced in 2021 to ensure that all three days of the weekend had context-heavy sessions that could affect the outcome of the Championship.
In the pre-Sprint era, the F1 race schedule had largely followed a similar format for decades – a few practice sessions on Friday, followed by another one on Saturday ahead of qualifying, and the all-important battle on Sunday.
It meant that most of the Friday running was for teams and drivers to fine-tune their cars and arrive at the ideal set-up. Often, teams didn’t even run in the first half hour of Friday’s first practice because the track was ‘dirty’.
The transformation
Sprints, by also offering Championship points, changed the equation. In the first two years of their existence, there was a seamless transition from one session to the next.
A single free practice on Friday was followed by a Sprint pole shootout (in the standard qualifying format) to set the grid for Saturday’s Sprint Qualifying (the 100km race). Saturday’s outcome set the grid for Sunday’s marquee contest, with the winner earning pole position.
However, it came with its own issues. Drivers were overly cautious in the Sprints to avoid damage that could hurt them in the main race. It also messed up some historical records, including what counted as a pole position.
In 2021, the winner of the Sprint Qualifying was given the pole stat. But with many, including the likes of Lewis Hamilton and Sebastian Vettel, believing that pole position should reflect single-lap prowess and not that of a mini-race, it was changed in 2022 to reward the fastest man in Friday’s shootout.
But that led to another paradox – the quickest on Friday would get the pole stat and the right to go first in the Sprint, but the top starter in Sunday’s main menu would still be the Sprint winner and not the pole-position holder.
Decoupling
To clear this confusion, world governing body FIA and F1, in 2023, decided to run Sprint as a standalone event on Saturdays, with its own qualifying called Sprint Shootout. Qualification for Sunday’s main race was held Friday evening.
In 2024, this stop-start, incoherent order was rectified by conducting the qualification for the Sprint on Friday, and the Sprint race first up on Saturday. Qualifying for Sunday’s blue-ribbon competition would follow.
F1’s rationale for adding programmes is positive fan feedback. “Since the Sprint was introduced in 2021, data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends,” the head honchos stated recently in a statement.
“Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than Free Practice; 82% of attendees at Sprint weekends say it adds value to their ticket; 75% of F1 fans believe Sprint events add greater value to a season’s calendar.”
Now that we are six years into the Sprint, it is a good time to explore what it has achieved.
Bitter-sweet
Every day of a Sprint weekend now has more purpose, and any competitive action is better than watching cars run by themselves.
But have these special occasions delivered anything memorable? Not much. In 2023, Max Verstappen clinched his third title at the Qatar GP Sprint, but that, for a purist, was a pedestrian way of crowning a World champion.
These contests haven’t been exciting because the format doesn’t differ much from a normal race day. Yes, there are no pit stops, which should enable drivers to race the wheels off to gain position.
However, that seldom happens, as the men behind the steering wheel are often risk-averse, especially if they are outside the points-scoring placings.
The racing maxim is that if faster cars start from behind, they will eventually move up, thereby building excitement. The 2005 Japanese GP, widely considered as one of the best races ever, is a good example.
Iconic drivers such as Michael Schumacher, Fernando Alonso and Kimi Raikkonen started 14th, 16th and 17th respectively, after a rain-affected qualifying session. Raikkonen and Alonso charged up to the front, with the former clinching victory through a sensational pass on the final lap while the latter came home third.
In the junior formulas below F1, the Sprint is often a reverse-grid competition where the fastest among the top-eight drivers starts eighth. It is designed that way to help developing drivers learn to pass cars and build wheel-to-wheel racing skills.
In F1, however, the overriding focus is fairness, for the stakes are much higher. This has led to the organisers being less bold.
Once the cars clear the first-lap jeopardy, Sprints often settle into a predictable rhythm, without even the strategic differences found in the main race.
While only a handful of drivers have won both the Sprint and the Grand Prix in the same weekend, there have not been many outlier winners or podium-finishers to build excitement in Sprints either.
Ways to improve
Now that F1 has decided to double down on Sprints, the sport needs to figure out how to make it a distinct and exciting product rather than a mini-Grand Prix.
Reverse grids are an option, but they could be problematic in places where overtaking is difficult, like Monaco, which incidentally is one of 10 Sprint events next season. Drivers do not seem enamoured by the idea, as they feel it could have a significant impact on the Championship table.
One way to jumble up the grids is to go back to one-shot qualifying, like in the early 2000s. In that format, drivers would go on to the track in a pre-determined order – Championship standings or results from the previous race – and get only one attempt to set their fastest lap. Even a small mistake could prove costly, or sudden rain during the session could trip them up.
F1 could also play around with tyre compounds. A bespoke, Sprint-specific compound that isn’t durable for the entire race can bring to the fore drivers’ tyre-management skills and spice up the racing, provided these events are run on tracks where overtaking is easier.
A 12% increase in viewership because of Sprints is indeed good, and the onus is now on F1 to do more to improve a product designed for spectacle than sporting purity. It is better to take a risk and fail than not try at all.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Gulveer secures silver; Baranica makes history; bronze for Manpreet
briefs.deck: Gulveer added yet another achievement to his kitty, winning silver in 28:29.38s, improving on his bronze from three years ago, in the 10,000m
briefs.bodyText:
It needs a touch of magic to share the spotlight with Gulveer Singh’s incredible consistency. On Friday (September 25, 2026), Baranica Elangovan managed to do so, soaring high and leaping into history as the first-ever Indian to win an Asian Games medal in pole vault.
The 29-year-old cleared a height of 4.15m to take joint bronze with Polina Ivanova of Kazakhstan at the Paloma Mizuho athletics stadium in Nagoya. It was nowhere close to her best, but it was enough to add India’s third medal from track and field on day two of the competition after Manpreet Kaur had finished third in shot put and Gulveer bettered his own performance with a silver in the 10,000m.
The other two are events that India has done reasonably well in in the past. Pole vault, meanwhile, is an outlier in Indian athletics; women’s vaulting even more so. Sindhushree, however, had a disappointing outing, ending with no mark against her name.
Gulveer, on the other hand, has redefined consistency when it comes to Indian athletics. As much as Neeraj Chopra has been the poster boy of Indian track and field, Gulveer comes close in terms of performances, if not necessarily in medals. On Friday (September 25), the 28-year-old added yet another achievement to his kitty, winning silver in 28:29.38s, improving on his bronze from three years ago.
The timing was far from his personal or even season’s best, but it hardly mattered. He could be in action three more times over the next few days, starting with the 1500m heats on Saturday (September 26), followed by the final and the 5000m.
India’s third medallist for the day, Manpreet, managed a best throw of 17.17m in her fourth attempt to end up on the podium behind the Chinese pair of Song Jiayuan (19.40) and Zhang Linru (18.14). Krishna Jayasankar came fifth with a best of 16.57m. Damneet Singh was ninth in hammer throw with 67.56 while Praveen Kumar threw 65.24 to finish 11th.
Meanwhile, both Indian sprinters in the men’s 100m crashed out in the semifinals — Gurindervir Singh clocking 10.32s and Animesh Kujur 10.38s — while the heptathletes too disappointed, Pooja ended sixth with 5,368 points and Anamika A.K. totalled 5,234 for eighth place.
Thailand’s Puripol Boonson stormed to the 100m title with a new Games record of 9.90s, the only one to go sub-10 throughout the competition, thrice while China’s Chen Yujie was crowned the continent’s fastest woman in 11.06.
Kiran Pahal (53.44) and Prachi (53.46) advanced to the final of the 400m, as did Vishal T.K. (45.27) among the men.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Couldn’t believe I had won a medal, says Baranica
briefs.deck: Even when my coach Milber Bertrand Russell told me to look up at the big screen for the official confirmation, I was not sure, I wanted him to confirm from the officials, said Baranica Elangovan
briefs.bodyText:
Baranica Elangovan won a historic first-ever bronze in pole vault at the Asian Games, but as long as it took for the event to finally conclude as Misaki Morota tried to cross the 4.61m mark, it took longer for the Indian to accept she had actually won a medal.
Also read | Persistence and drama as India’s mixed relay team, Seema win medals
“The other Indian pole vaulter, Sindhushree, told me I had won bronze, but I did not believe her. I kept checking again and again and again. Even when my coach Milber Bertrand Russell told me to look up at the big screen for the official confirmation, I was not sure, I wanted him to confirm from the officials. It is so surreal that I don’t think I will believe it till I actually get it in my hands,” a dazed but elated Baranica admitted.
Baranica’s medal came soon after Gulveer Singh, the man who runs like a machine and with as much consistency, improved on his bronze medal from Hangzhou 2023 with a silver in the 10,000m. With two more events he’s entered in, Gulveer was desperate to slip out for rest and recovery. Not surprisingly, he was more than satisfied with the medal. “I have no fixed target in terms of the timings because then I will get stuck on that. Only target is to win medals and keep improving,” an exhausted Gulveer said.
Shot-putter Manpreet Kaur, meanwhile, insisted there was more to come. “There is more to be done; I can get a lot better. But I am still learning a lot of new things under coach Parveer Singh in terms of technique, strength and throwing angles. He kept guiding me even today, suggesting changes that helped me get better,” she said.

briefs.bodyText:

Opting to bat, Golden Eagles were going at a steady rate before K. Pushpitha (91 n.o., 56b, 10x4, 4x6) brought out the fireworks – with P. briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Suruchi and Kamaljeet end India’s wait for a shooting gold
briefs.deck: The pair produces a new Asian and Games record in the 10m air pistol mixed team event; the men’s 50m rifle 3-position team of Tomar, Niraj and Rudrankksh bags silver
briefs.bodyText:
India’s wait for a shooting gold from the Aichi General Shooting Range finally ended on the sixth day of the competition. Suruchi Phogat and Kamaljeet combined to not only win the 10m air pistol mixed team event but also set a new Asian Games record in the process.
Keep track: Asian Games 2026 LIVE: India strikes gold in 10m air rifle mixed team final
Suruchi and Kamaljeet, having both shot ordinary scores in their respective individual events, made up for the disappointment as a team, totalling 484.6 points in the final. Suruchi, in particular, was in fine form and was largely responsible for keeping India ahead right from the start, first in the qualifying round and then in the final.
Suruchi shot a series of 99, 97 and a perfect 100 in the qualifying to total 296, the highest by any shooter, while Kamaljeet tried to keep pace with a 291. In the final round, Suruchi again kept getting as close to the middle as possible, consistently scoring in high 10s for 245.7 points. Kamaljeet could only manage 238.9 but together it was enough for gold and a new record.
India has already lost three of the seven golds it won in shooting last time around, although Friday’s (September 25, 2026) win made up for it a little. However, the 22-medal haul from Hangzhou now looks a far shot.
One of those golds that India failed to defend was in the men’s 50m 3-position team event, where it finished with a silver. Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, the joint owner of the qualifying Games record of 591, could only manage a 589. Niraj Kumar and Rudrankksh Patil shot 588 and 585, respectively, as the Indian trio managed a combined score of 1762, four behind China.
Tomar, also the Asian record holder and Niraj, however, disappointed in the individual event, finishing fifth and eighth, respectively. Tomar, silver medallist in the previous edition, was far from convincing, struggling to find his rhythm and the target in all three positions. With several of his shots scoring only nines, the 25-year-old had 102.9 in kneeling and 102.4 in prone for the first two rounds to trail top-placed and eventual champion Liu Yukun of China by 3.2 points. Yukun set a new Games record on way to his gold while compatriot Zhang Changhong took the silver.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: Gukesh’s brilliance helps India pip Germany; women crush Uzbekistan
briefs.bodyText:
After a while, India had a well-nigh perfect day at the Chess Olympiad. Both the men’s and women’s teams won their matches in the ninth round at Samarkand on Friday.
After conceding draws in the previous round, both teams had to win their matches. The men encountered a strong challenge from the giant-killer Germany before winning 2.5-1.5, while the women crushed host Uzbekistan 3-1.
The Indian men owe their win to World champion D. Gukesh, who showed resilience and brilliance to defeat Alexander Donchenko on the fourth board. He came back from an inferior position and found a superb knight manoeuvre on his way to a 54-move victory with black pieces.
The other games, featuring R. Praggnanandhaa, Arjun Erigaisi and Nihal Sarin were all drawn. India has 15 points and is in joint second position in the open section, along with Uzbekistan (2) and Armenia. With 16 points, Uzbekistan is in the sole lead. Just two rounds remain.
In the women’s event too, India is placed second with 15 points, alongside Kazakhstan and Mongolia. Former champion China is the sole leader with 17 points.
The Indian women were too good for Uzbekistan, though B. Savitha Shri, for the first time in the tournament, failed to win. After winning all her seven games, she was forced to split the point, with Guldona Karimova, but Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh and Vantika Agrawal won their games.

briefs.headline: Man City found guilty on all but one of 115 charges, reports say
briefs.deck: The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier ‌League ⁠board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, ⁠free from partisan influence, said the club in a statement
briefs.bodyText:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, the Athletic and the Times reported on Friday (September 25, 2026).
The club are expected to appeal, the reports added.
The Premier League declined to comment.
"It’s a confidential process, we’re not commenting at all," a spokesperson said.
City has maintained that the case had not yet been concluded.
"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality," the club said in a statement to British media.
"As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
If confirmed, the guilty verdict would represent one of the most significant rulings in English football history and mark a major development in a case that has overshadowed the league for more than three years.
The proceedings have raised questions about financial regulation, competitive integrity and how the league enforces its rules against its most successful clubs.
ALLEGATIONS SPANNING MORE THAN A DECADE
The Premier League referred City to an independent commission in February 2023 over alleged breaches of financial rules spanning the 2009-10 to 2022-23 seasons. The club have consistently denied wrongdoing.
Among the most serious allegations was that City failed in each season from 2009-10 to 2017-18 to provide accurate financial information giving a "true and fair view" of revenues, including sponsorship income, and operating costs.
City hired lawyer David Pannick to lead their defence, while the Premier League was represented by Adam Lewis KC, according to British media reports.
The hearing began on September 16, 2024, and concluded nearly three months later on December 6. The case was heard by an independent commission composed of three people appointed by the independent chair of the Premier League Judicial Panel.
City were banned from the Champions League for two years by European football's governing body UEFA in 2020 after being found to have overstated sponsorship revenue between 2012 and 2016. The club, however, successfully appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which overturned the ban.
Since Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group bought the club in 2008, City have won eight Premier League titles, the Champions League, four FA Cups and seven League Cups.
City top the Premier League after winning each of their opening five matches.
The stakes are particularly high because other clubs have already faced sporting sanctions for breaching financial regulations.
Everton were docked a total of eight points during the 2023-24 season after two separate breaches of the Premier League's Profitability and Sustainability Rules, while Nottingham Forest were deducted four points for a breach of the same rules in March 2024.
Newcastle United narrowly avoided potential sanctions after selling players before a June 30, 2024, financial reporting deadline to comply with spending regulations.
The allegations against City are far broader and cover more than a decade, making the case unprecedented in scale. Lawyers, club executives and supporters across the league have spent years awaiting a verdict.

briefs.headline: Hardik Pandya set to miss India A fixtures; racing against time for NZ tour
briefs.deck: The 32-year-old was inching closer to a return to cricket but the recurring shin issue has derailed all the progress he made at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in the last few months. I
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Hardik Pandya
's return to competitive cricket has been delayed again as the all-rounder is set to miss the three India A fixtures against Australia A in Puducherry starting October 6. The all-rounder experienced pain in his right shin again earlier this week and underwent a fresh set of scans. The BCCI medical team monitoring him has advised further rest.
The 32-year-old was inching closer to a return to cricket but the recurring shin issue has derailed all the progress he made at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in the last few months.
It was the same issue that ruled him out of selection for the Afghanistan T20Is. It is understood that he was also being considered for a late entry into the Asian Games but the unfortunate turn of events occurred close to selection day - first before the Afghanistan ODIs and then later for the T20Is against the same opposition.
With no physical activity for the next 10-15 days, it remains highly doubtful that Pandya will be available for the T20Is against New Zealand next month as well. The selectors would also operate with caution when considering him directly for the ODIs which follow the five T20Is. The team management's frustrating wait for their premier all-rounder continues, but they understand that a rushed approach will not be followed as the 2027 World Cup remains the ultimate goal.
There is no official word from the Indian cricket board yet. However, Suryansh Shedge is currently taining at the BCCI CoE and could well be drafted as 
Hardik
's replacement for three India A games.
